data.description: The main breaker panel and the GFCI outlets and AFCI breakers that protect the circuits.
data.name: Electrical panel, GFCI and AFCI

steps: Find each GFCI outlet (the ones with test and reset buttons), usually in kitchens, bathrooms, garage and outside.
Plug a lamp or night light into it and switch it on.
Press test: the light should go out.
Press reset: the light should come back on.
If it does not cut the power, stop using that outlet and call a licensed electrician.
tasks.title: Test the GFCI outlets
tasks.why: A GFCI cuts power in a fraction of a second if current leaks to ground, which protects against shock near water.

steps: Check the breaker label or manual for how often to test (often monthly).
Press the test button on each AFCI breaker: it should trip to off.
Switch it fully off and then back on to reset it.
If a breaker will not trip or will not reset, call a licensed electrician.
tasks.title: Test the AFCI breakers
tasks.why: AFCI breakers cut power when they sense arcing in wiring, a common start of electrical fires.

steps: Never remove the panel cover yourself; only open the small door to the breakers.
Clear boxes and storage from in front of the panel so it can be reached quickly.
Check every breaker has a clear label saying what it controls; fix any that are missing.
Look for scorch marks, a burning smell, buzzing or warm breakers; if you find any, call a licensed electrician.
tasks.title: Keep the electrical panel clear and labelled
tasks.why: In an emergency you need to reach and identify the right breaker fast.

steps: Hire a licensed electrician to inspect the panel and wiring.
Do not open the panel cover yourself; leave that to the electrician.
Ask them to check the panel, breakers, grounding and any old or aluminium wiring.
Ask whether GFCI or AFCI protection should be added anywhere.
Note what they found and anything they recommend fixing.
tasks.title: Book an electrical safety inspection
tasks.why: Wiring and panels age; an inspection finds loose connections and overloaded circuits before they cause a fire.

data.description: The valve that shuts off all water to the house.
data.name: Main water shutoff valve

steps: Tell everyone at home the water will be off for a minute.
Turn the valve slowly to closed, and check a tap to see the water stops.
Open the valve again slowly all the way.
Check the valve and its stem for drips afterwards.
If it is stuck or starts leaking, do not force it; call a plumber.
tasks.title: Exercise the main water shutoff valve
tasks.why: Valves that never move seize up; you want this one to work the first time a pipe bursts.

steps: Tie a clear tag on the valve saying it is the main water shutoff.
Make sure the path to it is clear of boxes and storage.
Show everyone at home where it is and which way turns it off.
Record the location in this item so it is in the house binder.
tasks.title: Label the main shutoff and show everyone
tasks.why: In a leak, the minutes spent finding the valve are the ones that cause the most damage.

data.description: A battery or hardwired smoke alarm.
data.name: Smoke alarm

steps: Tell everyone at home you are about to test the alarm.
Press and hold the test button until the alarm sounds.
If it stays silent or sounds weak, replace the battery and test again.
If it still fails, replace the alarm.
tasks.title: Test the smoke alarm
tasks.why: A working alarm gives you the minutes you need to get out in a fire.

steps: Have the right replacement battery ready.
Twist or slide the alarm off its base.
Swap the battery, matching the + and - marks.
Refit the alarm and press the test button.
tasks.title: Replace the smoke alarm battery
tasks.why: A low battery is the most common reason an alarm fails when it is needed.

steps: Check the date of manufacture on the back of the alarm.
Buy a replacement of the same type (and the same connector if hardwired).
For a hardwired alarm, switch off its circuit at the breaker first.
Fit the new alarm, restore power and press the test button.
Write the install date on the new alarm.
tasks.title: Replace the smoke alarm (ten-year life)
tasks.why: Smoke sensors wear out; alarms are meant to be replaced about every ten years.

steps: Use the soft brush attachment of a vacuum.
Gently vacuum the vents around the alarm cover.
Do not paint over or cover the alarm.
Press the test button afterwards.
tasks.title: Vacuum the smoke alarm vents
tasks.why: Dust in the sensing chamber causes false alarms, which tempt people to disable alarms.

steps: Put a few drops of food colouring in each toilet tank.
Wait about 15 minutes without flushing.
If colour shows in the bowl, the flapper is leaking and should be replaced.
Flush afterwards so the dye does not stain.
tasks.title: Dye-test the toilets for silent leaks
tasks.why: A leaking flapper can waste a lot of water without making a sound.

steps: Flush and watch the tank refill: it should stop by itself below the overflow tube.
If water keeps running into the overflow, adjust or replace the fill valve.
Turn the shutoff valve behind the toilet off and on again to keep it working.
Check the supply line and valve for drips; replace a worn plastic supply line with a braided one.
tasks.title: Check the toilet fill valve and shutoff
tasks.why: A working shutoff stops an overflow fast, and a running fill valve wastes water all day.

steps: Gently push the toilet side to side: it should not move.
Look and feel for damp, staining or soft flooring around the base.
If it rocks or leaks, stop using it and call a plumber or reset it on a new wax ring.
tasks.title: Check the toilet bases for leaks and rocking
tasks.why: A slow leak under a toilet quietly rots the subfloor.

data.description: The caulk and grout around bathtubs and showers.
data.name: Tub and shower caulk and grout

steps: Look along every caulk line for cracks, gaps, peeling or black mould underneath.
Check grout lines for cracks or missing pieces.
Press on tiles near the tub: they should not move or sound hollow.
Note anything that needs recaulking or regrouting.
tasks.title: Inspect the tub and shower caulk and grout
tasks.why: Water that gets behind tiles or the tub edge rots the wall and floor without showing.

steps: Cut and scrape out all the old caulk with a plastic scraper or caulk tool.
Clean the joint, kill any mould, and let it dry fully, ideally overnight.
Run a steady bead of bathroom silicone caulk along the joint.
Smooth it with a wet finger or tool and wipe off the excess.
Leave the shower unused for as long as the caulk label says.
tasks.title: Recaulk the tub or shower
tasks.why: Fresh caulk on a dry, clean joint keeps water out of the wall.

data.description: The supply lines, shutoff valves and drains under every sink.
data.name: Pipes under sinks

steps: Empty or move what is stored under each sink so you can see.
Run the tap for a minute and watch the drain and supply joints for drips.
Feel the cabinet floor for damp and look for stains, swelling or mould.
Tighten a dripping drain nut by hand; call a plumber for anything else.
tasks.title: Look under every sink for leaks
tasks.why: Small leaks under sinks go unnoticed for months and ruin cabinets and floors.

steps: Check each flexible supply line for bulges, kinks, rust or cracks.
Replace plain plastic or rubber lines with braided stainless lines.
Turn each shutoff valve off and on again to keep it from seizing.
If a valve is stuck or leaks, do not force it; call a plumber.
tasks.title: Check the sink supply lines and shutoff valves
tasks.why: Supply lines are under constant pressure, and a burst line floods fast.

data.description: Outside windows and doors, their seals and locks.
data.name: Windows and doors

steps: On a windy day, hold a lit incense stick or a strip of tissue near window and door edges to find drafts.
Look for weatherstripping that is torn, flat or missing.
Replace worn weatherstripping and fit door sweeps where light shows under doors.
Seal gaps between frames and walls with caulk.
tasks.title: Check window and door weatherstripping
tasks.why: Sealing air leaks around windows and doors is one of the cheapest ways to cut heating and cooling bills.

steps: Lock and unlock each outside door: the bolt should slide fully home.
Check each window latch closes and holds the sash tight.
Tighten loose screws on strike plates and latches.
Repair or replace locks that stick or do not catch.
tasks.title: Check window and door locks
tasks.why: Locks that work smoothly get used, and sticking ones get left open.

steps: Open each bedroom and basement escape window fully.
Make sure it is not painted or nailed shut and opens without tools.
Check that window bars or security grilles have a quick-release inside.
Go over the home fire escape plan with everyone while you are at it.
tasks.title: Check every bedroom window opens for escape
tasks.why: In a fire, a window may be the second way out; it must open quickly.

value.title: Inspect the tub and shower caulk and grout
value.why: Water that gets behind tiles or the tub edge rots the wall and floor without showing.

steps: Cut and scrape out all the old caulk with a plastic scraper or caulk tool.
Clean the joint, kill any mould, and let it dry fully, ideally overnight.
Run a steady bead of bathroom silicone caulk along the joint.
Smooth it with a wet finger or tool and wipe off the excess.
Leave the shower unused for as long as the caulk label says.
value.title: Recaulk the tub or shower
value.why: Fresh caulk on a dry, clean joint keeps water out of the wall.

operations.value: Outside windows and doors, their seals and locks.

steps: On a windy day, hold a lit incense stick or a strip of tissue near window and door edges to find drafts.
Look for weatherstripping that is torn, flat or missing.
Replace worn weatherstripping and fit door sweeps where light shows under doors.
Seal gaps between frames and walls with caulk.
value.title: Check window and door weatherstripping
value.why: Sealing air leaks around windows and doors is one of the cheapest ways to cut heating and cooling bills.

steps: Lock and unlock each outside door: the bolt should slide fully home.
Check each window latch closes and holds the sash tight.
Tighten loose screws on strike plates and latches.
Repair or replace locks that stick or do not catch.
value.title: Check window and door locks
value.why: Locks that work smoothly get used, and sticking ones get left open.

steps: Open each bedroom and basement escape window fully.
Make sure it is not painted or nailed shut and opens without tools.
Check that window bars or security grilles have a quick-release inside.
Go over the home fire escape plan with everyone while you are at it.
value.title: Check every bedroom window opens for escape
value.why: In a fire, a window may be the second way out; it must open quickly.
